summary.text: Induction through the order- recurrence gives a quadratic closed form with a period- correction, which residue-by-residue is equivalent to the stated floor polynomial. Monotone upper and lower Euler–Maclaurin-type bounds for \(H_m-\log m-\gamma\), obtained from truncated \(\operatorname{artanh}\) expansions, combine with positive rational inequalities in each residue class to show \(1/(a(n)+1)<2H_n-H_{n^2+n-1}-\gamma\le 1/a(n)\), forcing the desired floor.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_m=\sum_{j=1}^m\frac1j,
\qquad
\gamma=\lim_{m\to\infty}(H_m-\log m).
\]
We prove that, for every integer \(n\geq 1\),
\[
a(n)=\left\lfloor\frac1{2H_n-H_{n^2+n-1}-\gamma}\right\rfloor.
\]
The proof has three parts: first we identify the sequence explicitly; next we obtain sufficiently sharp uniform bounds for the harmonic-number expression; finally we compare those bounds with the explicit integer value of the sequence.

## 1. The closed form of the sequence

It is convenient first to use zero-based indexing. Let \(b_m=a(m+1)\). Thus
\[
b_0,b_1,\ldots,b_6=2,7,14,23,35,50,67,
\]
and the order-seven recurrence for A227582 is
\[
b_{m+7}=b_m-2b_{m+1}+b_{m+2}-b_{m+5}+2b_{m+6}.
\tag{1}
\]
Define the period-five correction
\[
c(r)=
\begin{cases}
10,&r=0,\\
11,&r=1,\\
10,&r=2,\\
7,&r=3,4.
\end{cases}
\]
We claim that
\[
5b_m=6m^2+18m+c(m\bmod 5).
\tag{2}
\]
For \(m=0,1,\ldots,6\), direct substitution gives respectively
\[
10,35,70,115,175,250,335=5(2,7,14,23,35,50,67),
\]
so (2) holds initially.

Suppose now that it is known for all indices through \(m+6\). Multiply (1) by \(5\) and substitute (2) at the five indices \(m,m+1,m+2,m+5,m+6\). The quadratic parts combine to the quadratic part at \(m+7\). This can be checked by expanding, or equivalently by observing that the linear combination in (1) has the appropriate zeroth, first, and second moments for a quadratic sequence. For the periodic corrections, periodicity gives
\[
c(m+5)=c(m),\qquad c(m+6)=c(m+1),\qquad c(m+7)=c(m+2),
\]
and therefore
\[
c(m)-2c(m+1)+c(m+2)-c(m+5)+2c(m+6)=c(m+2)=c(m+7).
\]
Thus (2) follows by induction.

Put \(m=n-1\) in (2). After expansion,
\[
b_{n-1}=\frac{6n^2+6n+c((n-1)\bmod5)-12}{5}.
\tag{3}
\]
Splitting according to \(n\bmod5\), this says
\[
a(n)=b_{n-1}=
\begin{cases}
(6n^2+6n-5)/5,&n\equiv0,4\pmod5,\\
(6n^2+6n-2)/5,&n\equiv1,3\pmod5,\\
(6n^2+6n-1)/5,&n\equiv2\pmod5.
\end{cases}
\tag{4}
\]
These are exactly the five residue cases for
\[
a(n)=\left\lfloor\frac{6n^2+6n-1}{5}\right\rfloor.
\tag{5}
\]
In particular, all the quantities in (4) are nonnegative for \(n\ge1\).

## 2. Bounds for the harmonic-number error

Define
\[
\psi(x)=H_x-\log x-\gamma
\]
when \(x\) is a positive integer. We shall prove the uniform bounds
\[
s_4(x)<\psi(x)<s_3(x),
\tag{6}
\]
where, for real \(x\ge1\),
\[
s_3(x)=\frac1{2x}-\frac1{12x^2}+\frac1{120x^4},
\qquad
s_4(x)=s_3(x)-\frac1{252x^6}.
\tag{7}
\]

We begin with the logarithmic estimates that imply (6). For \(0\le z<1\), the identity
\[
\log\frac{1+z}{1-z}=2\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^{2j+1}}{2j+1}
\tag{8}
\]
has positive terms. Consequently,
\[
2\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{z^{2j+1}}{2j+1}
\le \log\frac{1+z}{1-z}
\le
2\left(\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\frac{z^{2j+1}}{2j+1}
       +\frac{z^{2r+1}}{1-z^2}\right).
\tag{9}
\]
The upper estimate follows because every denominator in the omitted tail is at least \(1\), so that the tail is at most the corresponding geometric series. Strictness in the comparisons below follows from positivity of further terms.

For \(K\ge1\), take \(z=1/(2K+1)\). Then
\[
\frac{1+z}{1-z}=\frac{K+1}{K}.
\]
Using the upper bound in (9) through the powers \(z,z^3,z^5\), we obtain
\[
\log\frac{K+1}{K}
\le 2\left(z+\frac{z^3}{3}+\frac{z^5}{5}+\frac{z^7}{1-z^2}\right).
\tag{10}
\]
A common-denominator calculation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left[\frac1{K+1}-\left(\frac1{2(K+1)}-\frac1{2K}\right)
 +\left(\frac1{12(K+1)^2}-\frac1{12K^2}\right)
 -\left(\frac1{120(K+1)^4}-\frac1{120K^4}\right)\right]\\
&\quad-2\left(z+\frac{z^3}{3}+\frac{z^5}{5}+\frac{z^7}{1-z^2}\right)\\
&=\frac{40K^6+120K^5+182K^4+164K^3+76K^2+14K+1}
{120K^4(K+1)^4(2K+1)^5}>0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
Thus
\[
\log\frac{K+1}{K}<
\frac1{K+1}-\left(\frac1{2(K+1)}-\frac1{2K}\right)
+\left(\frac1{12(K+1)^2}-\frac1{12K^2}\right)
-\left(\frac1{120(K+1)^4}-\frac1{120K^4}\right).
\tag{12}
\]

Likewise, the lower bound in (9), now through \(z^7/7\), and the identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
&2\left(z+\frac{z^3}{3}+\frac{z^5}{5}+\frac{z^7}{7}\right)\\
&\quad-\left[\frac1{K+1}-\left(\frac1{2(K+1)}-\frac1{2K}\right)
+\left(\frac1{12(K+1)^2}-\frac1{12K^2}\right)
-\left(\frac1{120(K+1)^4}-\frac1{120K^4}\right)
+\left(\frac1{252(K+1)^6}-\frac1{252K^6}\right)\right]\\
&=\frac{10612K^{10}+53060K^9+119322K^8+158928K^7+138774K^6+82926K^5
+34317K^4+9720K^3+1809K^2+200K+10}
{2520K^6(K+1)^6(2K+1)^7}>0
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]
give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac1{K+1}-\left(\frac1{2(K+1)}-\frac1{2K}\right)
+\left(\frac1{12(K+1)^2}-\frac1{12K^2}\right)
-\left(\frac1{120(K+1)^4}-\frac1{120K^4}\right)\\
&\qquad+\left(\frac1{252(K+1)^6}-\frac1{252K^6}\right)
<\log\frac{K+1}{K}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
Every denominator in (11) and (13) is positive for \(K\ge1\), and every coefficient in the numerator is positive, proving the displayed signs.

Now define, for positive integers \(k\),
\[
P_k=H_k-\log k-\frac1{2k}+\frac1{12k^2}-\frac1{120k^4},
\qquad
Q_k=P_k+\frac1{252k^6}.
\tag{15}
\]
Since \(H_{k+1}-H_k=1/(k+1)\), subtracting consecutive terms in (15) shows that (12) is precisely the assertion
\[
P_{k+1}-P_k>0.
\]
Thus \((P_k)\) is strictly increasing. Similarly, (14) is precisely
\[
Q_{k+1}-Q_k<0,
\]
so \((Q_k)\) is strictly decreasing.

By the definition of \(\gamma\), \(H_k-\log k\to\gamma\), while all the correction terms in (15) tend to zero. Hence
\[
P_k\to\gamma,
\qquad Q_k\to\gamma.
\]
A strictly increasing sequence converging to \(\gamma\) lies strictly below \(\gamma\), and a strictly decreasing sequence converging to \(\gamma\) lies strictly above it. Therefore
\[
P_k<\gamma<Q_k \qquad(k\ge1).
\tag{16}
\]
Rearranging the left and right inequalities in (16) yields exactly
\[
s_4(k)<H_k-\log k-\gamma<s_3(k),
\]
which proves (6).

## 3. Bounds tailored to the required expression

Fix \(n\ge1\), regard \(N=n\) as a real number, and put
\[
M=N^2+N-1.
\]
Thus \(M\ge1\). Define
\[
D=2H_n-H_{n^2+n-1}-\gamma.
\tag{17}
\]
Using \(H_k=\log k+\gamma+\psi(k)\), we can rewrite this as
\[
D=2\psi(N)-\psi(M)-L(N),
\qquad
L(N)=\log M-2\log N.
\tag{18}
\]
We next bound \(L(N)\) by the same logarithmic series. Set
\[
S=(N+1)(2N-1),
\qquad x=\frac{N-1}{S}.
\]
For \(N\ge1\), \(S>0\) and \(0\le x<1\). Direct algebra gives
\[
\frac{1+x}{1-x}=\frac{N^2+N-1}{N^2},
\]
and hence, by (8),
\[
L(N)=\log\frac{1+x}{1-x}.
\]
Define
\[
T_{\rm lo}(N)=2\left(x+\frac{x^3}{3}\right)
\tag{19}
\]
and
\[
T_{\rm hi}(N)=T_{\rm lo}(N)+
\frac{(N-1)^5}{2N^2(N^2+N-1)S^3}.
\tag{20}
\]
The lower estimate in (9), through \(x^3/3\), gives
\[
T_{\rm lo}(N)\le L(N).
\tag{21}
\]
For the upper estimate, (9) gives a remainder \(2x^5/(1-x^2)\). The algebraic identity
\[
1-x^2=\frac{4N^2(N^2+N-1)}{S^2}
\]
shows that
\[
\frac{2x^5}{1-x^2}
=\frac{(N-1)^5}{2N^2(N^2+N-1)S^3}.
\]
Thus
\[
L(N)\le T_{\rm hi}(N).
\tag{22}
\]

We also need one slight weakening of the lower harmonic-error bound at \(M\). Define
\[
p(M)=\frac1{2M}-\frac1{12M^2}.
\]
For every \(M\ge1\),
\[
p(M)<s_4(M).
\tag{23}
\]
Indeed,
\[
s_4(M)-p(M)=\frac1{120M^4}-\frac1{252M^6}>0,
\]
because \(252M^6>120M^4\) for \(M\ge1\).

Now define the two explicit rational functions
\[
D_{\rm hi}(N)=2s_3(N)-p(M)-T_{\rm lo}(N),
\tag{24}
\]
\[
D_{\rm lo}(N)=2s_4(N)-s_3(M)-T_{\rm hi}(N).
\tag{25}
\]
From (6), (21), and (23),
\[
\psi(N)<s_3(N),\qquad \psi(M)>s_4(M)>p(M),\qquad L(N)\ge T_{\rm lo}(N).
\]
Substitution into (18) gives the strict upper bound
\[
D<D_{\rm hi}(N).
\tag{26}
\]
Similarly, (6) and (22) give
\[
\psi(N)>s_4(N),\qquad \psi(M)<s_3(M),\qquad L(N)\le T_{\rm hi}(N),
\]
and therefore
\[
D_{\rm lo}(N)<D.
\tag{27}
\]

It remains to compare these rational bounds with the three possible formulas in (4). For \(q\in\{1,2,5\}\), put
\[
A_q(N)=\frac{6N^2+6N-q}{5}.
\tag{28}
\]
The required rational inequalities are
\[
A_q(N)D_{\rm hi}(N)\le1,
\qquad
1<(A_q(N)+1)D_{\rm lo}(N)
\quad(N\ge1).
\tag{29}
\]
For completeness, these follow from the following explicit positive-coefficient calculations. Write \(N=1+e\), where \(e\ge0\). On substituting (7), (19), (20), (24), and (25), putting terms over common denominators, one obtains
\[
1-A_q(1+e)D_{\rm hi}(1+e)=\frac{U_q(e)}{R_q(e)},
\qquad
(A_q(1+e)+1)D_{\rm lo}(1+e)-1=\frac{V_q(e)}{S_q(e)},
\tag{30}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_5&=300(e+1)^4(e+2)^3(2e+1)^3(e^2+3e+1)^2,\\
R_2&=150(e+1)^4(e+2)^3(2e+1)^3(e^2+3e+1)^2,\\
R_1&=300(e+1)^4(e+2)^3(2e+1)^3(e^2+3e+1)^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_5(e)={}&944+15240e+108524e^2+450082e^3+1208830e^4+2211299e^5\\
&+2820338e^6+2523110e^7+1569534e^8+661856e^9+179728e^{10}+28268e^{11}+1952e^{12},\\
U_2(e)={}&160+2688e+19624e^2+82748e^3+224936e^4+415375e^5+533815e^6\\
&+480367e^7+300054e^8+126856e^9+34502e^{10}+5434e^{11}+376e^{12},\\
U_1(e)={}&112+2088e+16156e^2+70634e^3+196886e^4+370567e^5+483394e^6\\
&+439942e^7+276966e^8+117664e^9+32096e^{10}+5068e^{11}+352e^{12}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the second identity in (30),
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_5&=2100(e+1)^5(e+2)^2(2e+1)^3(e^2+3e+1)^4,\\
S_2&=4200(e+1)^6(e+2)^3(2e+1)^3(e^2+3e+1)^4,\\
S_1&=6300(e+1)^6(e+2)^3(2e+1)^3(e^2+3e+1)^4,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_5(e)={}&8+996e+15302e^2+115115e^3+539334e^4+1729919e^5+3970228e^6\\
&+6658089e^7+8231758e^8+7519367e^9+5066430e^{10}+2509178e^{11}\\
&+909860e^{12}+240144e^{13}+45116e^{14}+5544e^{15}+336e^{16},\\
V_2(e)={}&8440+206628e+2310602e^2+15720079e^3+72974164e^4+245417429e^5\\
&+619334522e^6+1198351651e^7+1801097980e^8+2117500561e^9\\
&+1951535468e^{10}+1406611604e^{11}+787215628e^{12}+337615036e^{13}\\
&+108597464e^{14}+25304604e^{15}+4026976e^{16}+391104e^{17}+17472e^{18},\\
V_1(e)={}&16864+411240e+4587604e^2+31163026e^3+144509013e^4+485641903e^5\\
&+1224999497e^6+2369746521e^7+3561787949e^8+4188609025e^9\\
&+3862148217e^{10}+2785486195e^{11}+1560017572e^{12}+669511026e^{13}\\
&+215474404e^{14}+50222628e^{15}+7991532e^{16}+775656e^{17}+34608e^{18}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All factors in the six denominators are positive for \(e\ge0\), and all coefficients in the six numerators are positive. Hence both fractions in (30) are positive (the first could even be weakened to nonnegative), proving (29).

## 4. The final floor comparison

Let \(K=a(n)\), regarded first as an integer and then as a real number. According to (4), there is a \(q\in\{1,2,5\}\) such that
\[
K=A_q(N):
\]
namely,
\[
q=5\quad(n\equiv0,4\pmod5),\qquad
q=2\quad(n\equiv1,3\pmod5),\qquad
q=1\quad(n\equiv2\pmod5).
\]
Also \(K\ge0\). Combining (26), (27), and (29), we get
\[
K D_{\rm hi}\le1,
\qquad
1<(K+1)D_{\rm lo},
\qquad
D_{\rm lo}<D<D_{\rm hi}.
\tag{31}
\]
First, (31) forces \(D_{\rm lo}>0\): if \(D_{\rm lo}\le0\), then \(K+1>0\) would give \((K+1)D_{\rm lo}\le0\), contrary to the second inequality. Hence \(D>0\).

Because \(K\ge0\) and \(D<D_{\rm hi}\), the first inequality in (31) gives
\[
KD<KD_{\rm hi}\le1,
\]
with the harmless possibility of equality at the left when \(K=0\); in all cases \(KD\le1\). Since \(D>0\), this is equivalent to
\[
K\le\frac1D.
\tag{32}
\]
Likewise, from \(D_{\rm lo}<D\) and \(K+1>0\),
\[
1<(K+1)D_{\rm lo}<(K+1)D,
\]
so
\[
\frac1D<K+1.
\tag{33}
\]
Together, (32) and (33) say
\[
K\le\frac1D<K+1.
\]
Since \(K\) is an integer,
\[
K=\left\lfloor\frac1D\right\rfloor.
\]
Finally, substituting the definition (17) of \(D\) gives
\[
\boxed{
 a(n)=\left\lfloor\frac{1}{2H_n-H_{n^2+n-1}-\gamma}\right\rfloor
}
\qquad(n\ge1),
\]
as required.
